book.title: The Road to the Hearth-Hall
book.author: Edwy Marten
pages:
Edwy Marten of Larkfold, thatcher. Two winters since the raiders came down off the moor and burned Larkfold, and I am the last of us still walking.

In this pot is a coal from the Larkfold hearth. I have kept it alive under ash two winters, a handful of charcoal a night. In this fold of paper are our dead, twenty-two names. I am carrying both to the hearth-hall, where her fire never goes out, so the Hearthkeeper remembers us.

Cass is not on the list. I will not put her on it.

At a drovers' fire I met a man called Hollin who knows the ways. He says there is a girl in the raiders' camp on the moor, about seventeen, red hair, who will not give her name. He says the camp will sell her back. He says it like a man who has done it before.

I gave him my purse to carry the asking. He came back in four days. They want more.

Hollin says the camp will not deal with him twice. I must go myself, with the rest of it, at the new moon. He will show me the way as far as the old ditch.

I have put the pot and the names under the waystone at the fork, in case. If the coal goes out it is not ours any more, the hall-keepers say. It has a day or two in it, under the ash. Somebody find it before then.

Bitten. At the ditch, by one of the fresh dead, a woman in a Larkfold shawl. I think it was Ada Wren. I think she knew me.

Hollin ran with the purse. Of course he did.

It burns up the arm. I know what comes now. If I stand up again it will not be me.

The pot. The names. The hall. And tell Cass her father came. Tell her I came.

drovers.name: the drovers' fire at the old sheepwash

camp.name: the raiders' camp on the moor

ditch.name: the old ditch below the moor

hollow.name: a hollow under the moor's edge

grave.name: a stone at the camp's edge

to_fork.journal: A diary came off one of the fresh dead. Edwy Marten of Larkfold was carrying a coal from his burned village's hearth, and the names of its dead, to a hearth-hall. He went to buy his daughter Cass back from a raiders' camp, and was bitten on the way. He hid the pot and the names under a waystone.

clues.name: A clay hearth-pot
lore: Lidded, packed with ash, a thumb's width of charcoal on top.
Cold all through. Whatever was alive in it went out a long time ago.
clues.journal: The hearth-pot was under the waystone. The coal in it was cold.

clues.name: Twenty-two names
lore: Folded in oilcloth. A miller, a smith, the Wren girls, three Martens.
At the bottom, a name was written and scratched out so hard the pen went through.
clues.journal: The names of Larkfold's twenty-two dead were folded with it. One more had been written at the bottom and scratched out.

clues.name: A half-carved bird
lore: Alder, whittled by firelight. The wings are done and the head is not.
C. is cut on the base, small, the way a father marks a thing for a child.
clues.journal: There was a little wooden bird, half carved, marked C.

clues.name: A pouch of charcoal
lore: A handful a night, the diary said. There is a handful left.
He meant to come back for it.
clues.journal: A pouch of charcoal lay with the pot. He had meant to come back before the coal starved.

say: A hearth-pot. Larkfold? I remember Larkfold. They brought their coal here every midwinter, a thatcher and his girl, to light it new from ours. The girl always wanted to carry it and was never let.
It is cold. Oh. It is cold. A cold coal is not a hearth any more. It is a stone. She will not know it.

replies.say: Can it be lit again?
The thatcher is dead. He asked for this.

say: From our fire, yes, by a hand of that hearth. Kin. The names said aloud by somebody who knew the faces. A stranger can carry the pot. A stranger cannot be Larkfold.
If no kin is left, then the stranger says the names, and she hears a stranger, and she does what she can with that. It is something. It is not the same.
And you said Hollin. I know Hollin. He brings grieving folk to my door, and then he takes them away again to this camp or that. I have never once seen him bring anybody back.

replies.say: Then I'll find Cass.
replies.journal: {keeper} of the hearth-hall said the Larkfold coal could be lit again from the Hearthkeeper's fire, but only kin could truly say the names. She knew Hollin: he led grieving folk away and never brought anybody back.

replies.say: Then I'll start with Hollin.
replies.journal: {keeper} of the hearth-hall said the Larkfold coal could be lit again from the Hearthkeeper's fire, but only kin could truly say the names. Hollin was known to her, and not well.

replies.say: Keep the pot. Say the names yourself.
replies.journal: The hearth-pot and the names were left with {keeper}.

say: Another one with a look on them. Sit by the fire, friend, it is free. Most things are not.
Edwy Marten? A thatcher? I do not know the name. I meet a great many folk and I do not keep their names, it is kinder. Oh. That is his book. Well.

replies.say: He wrote that you ran with his purse.
Tell me about the girl in the camp.

?cass=held: I ran. The dead came up out of the ditch and I ran, and so would you. The purse was in my hand when I ran. I did not think to throw it back.

The girl is real, if that is what you are asking. Red hair, will not give her name. The camp keeps her for the cooking and the mending, and she has run twice. They will sell her, at a price. I can take you to the asking, for a share.
?cass=wed: I ran. The dead came up out of the ditch and I ran, and so would you. The purse was in my hand when I ran. I did not think to throw it back.

The girl is real. I did not tell him the rest of it. She is with one of them now, by her own choosing, and there is a baby on her hip. What was I to say to a man with a coal in a pot? I told him what he could carry.
?: I ran. The dead came up out of the ditch and I ran, and so would you. The purse was in my hand when I ran. I did not think to throw it back.

The girl. There was a girl, the first winter. Red hair. She died at the turn of the year, of the cough. I told him she lived because he would not have paid for a grave. I am not proud of it. I am not anything any more.

journal.?cass=held: Hollin owned that he ran from the ditch with Edwy's purse. He said the red-haired girl was alive in the camp, kept for work, and that the camp would sell her.
journal.?cass=wed: Hollin owned that he ran from the ditch with Edwy's purse. He said the red-haired girl had taken up with one of the raiders by her own choosing, and had a baby. He never told her father.
journal.?: Hollin owned that he ran from the ditch with Edwy's purse. He said the red-haired girl died of the cough the first winter, and that he told her father she lived because a grave would not pay.

replies.say: That purse was a dying man's. Hand it over.
Show me the way to the camp, and keep your share.
replies.journal: Hollin was paid in the dead man's coin to show the way to the camp on the moor.

replies.say: Get out of my sight.
replies.journal: Hollin was let go with Edwy's purse.

fight_hollin.taunt: Everybody always wants something off Hollin.
fight_hollin.plea: All right! All right. It is yours, take it, I yield. I am no fighter, look at me.
fight_hollin.mercy: The purse, and the way to the camp.
fight_hollin.thanks: The purse, and the way. And then I am off this road. I swear it on my mother's hearth.

spared_returns.say: I have been thinking about that thatcher. I have led a lot of folk up onto that moor, and you are the first I ever saw go up there for somebody else and not for what was owed them. I never once went back for anybody. I would like to learn how it is done. I know every drove road and every ditch from here to the hills.

clues.name: A thatcher's purse
lore: Stitched with straw-coloured thread, as a thatcher would.
Nearly empty. Hollin has been eating well.
clues.journal: Edwy Marten's purse was in Hollin's pack, nearly empty.

clues.name: A list in Hollin's hand
lore: Seven names, each with a sum beside it and a camp.
Every one has a line through it. None of them has a second sum.
clues.journal: Hollin kept a list of seven grieving folk he had taken money from. None of them ever got anybody back.

clues.name: A red ribbon
lore: A girl's hair ribbon, faded, with a Larkfold knot in it.
Proof to show a father. He never showed it. It would have meant going back up.
clues.journal: Hollin had a girl's ribbon with a Larkfold knot in it, taken from the camp as proof and never shown.

clues.name: A braided cord
lore: Red hair and black braided together, the way the moor camps tie a wedding.
Cut short with a knife. Somebody's keepsake, stolen.
clues.journal: Hollin had a wedding cord of red hair and black, the way the moor camps tie one, cut from somebody.

clues.name: A curl of red hair
lore: In a twist of cloth, with grave dirt still in it.
Something to sell to a grieving father, later, at a better price.
clues.journal: Hollin had a curl of red hair in a twist of cloth, with grave dirt on it.

lines: I have kept a place in the hearth for Larkfold, swept and ready, and I put a little salt on it every night so she knows it is spoken for.

Drovers came through yesterday. They say the dead are walking below the moor at the old ditch, a crowd of them together, in smocks and shawls, the way a village walks out to its fields. One of the women wears a shawl with a wren worked on it.
The camp on the moor only deals at the new moon, they say. That is tomorrow night.

ditch_dead.journal: Larkfold's dead were walking at the old ditch, in their smocks and shawls, and were put down. One woman's shawl had a wren worked on it.

?cass=held: You came up the moor alone, past the lookout, with your hands where we could see them. Either you are mad or you are buying.
The red-haired one. Yes. She mends and she cooks and she does not talk, and she has run twice. Her price is what it is.
?cass=wed: You came up the moor alone, past the lookout, with your hands where we could see them. Either you are mad or you are somebody's kin.
Cass. Yes. She is mine and I am hers, and the boy is ours. If you have come to take her down to a burned village, you can try asking her. I would not try anything else.
?: You came up the moor alone, past the lookout, with your hands where we could see them. Either you are mad or you are somebody's kin.
The red-haired girl. She died the first winter, of the cough, in my sister's tent. We are not everything the towns say. We put her in the ground at the camp's edge with a stone on her.

replies.say: Edwy Marten was her father. He died on the way up here.
Hollin had her father's purse off him and never came up.

?cass=held: Her father. The one Hollin kept coming about. Hollin had his coin off him twice and never once brought it up the moor. So that is how it is.
{coins:25}, or eight iron, or take her off me with a blade and see what my people make of it. Those are the ways out of this camp. Go and tell her, if you like. She will not believe you.
?cass=wed: Her father. She will want to know that, and she will not want to hear it from me. She is at the tents. Go and say it.
?: Hollin came up asking after her, after. Wanting a lock of her hair to sell to somebody. I gave him nothing, so I expect he dug for it. Her stone is at the camp's edge. Go and see it. Then go.

replies.say: Let me see her.

?cass=held: You are not from the camp. You walk like a town. Who sent you? Nobody sends anybody for me.

My father. He came? He came all this way, with the pot? Where is he? No. Do not say it. I can see it on you. Take me down. Take me to the hall. I will say their names if it is the last thing I do with my mouth.
?: You are not from the camp. You walk like a town. Who sent you?

My father. He came? He came all this way, with the pot. And Hollin. Oh, I know Hollin. I'll not go back to Larkfold. There is no Larkfold. There is this, and him, and the boy. But I will go down to the hall and say their names, if you walk me there, and then I come back up. Promise me that, or I'll not take one step.

journal.?cass=held: Cass Marten was alive in the camp, kept for work. She asked to be taken down to the hall to say the names.
journal.?: Cass Marten was alive in the camp and had a man and a baby there by her own choosing. She would go down to the hall to say the names, if she was walked back up after.

replies.say: {coins:25} to {raider}, and you walk out free.
replies.journal: Cass Marten was bought out of the camp for {coins:25}.

replies.say: I'll bring {raider} his eight iron.
We go now. If he stops us, he stops a blade.
I promise. Down to the hall, and back up again.
replies.journal: Cass was promised that she would be walked down to the hall and back up again to her own fire.

replies.say: Then I'll carry the names down alone.
replies.journal: Cass was left at the camp, and the names were carried down alone.

bring_iron.journal: Cass Marten was bought out of the camp for eight iron.

camp_fight.taunt: Then come and stop me, town. Up, lads!
camp_fight.plea: Enough. Enough! Take her, take the girl, I yield. My people are watching. Finish it or go.
camp_fight.thanks: Nobody follows. Go on, then. Go, before I change my mind in front of them.

spared_returns.say: You put me on my back in front of my own camp and let me get up. Do you know what a camp does with a man it has seen spared? It stops listening to him. I have nobody now. I have only these few, and they came because I promised them you.

clues.name: A stone at the camp's edge
lore: A plain grey stone set upright. Somebody has scratched a C on it, badly, as if they did not know their letters and asked.
The turf at its foot has been cut and put back. Recently.
clues.journal: Cass Marten's grave was at the camp's edge under a plain stone with a C scratched on it. The turf had been cut and put back.

clues.name: A candle stub
lore: Burned down to nothing, in a hollow in the turf.
Somebody in the camp has been lighting it. There are a great many drips.
clues.journal: Somebody in the camp had been lighting a candle at her grave, many nights.

clues.name: A rag of Larkfold weave
lore: Red and grey, in the Larkfold check, tied to a stick at the head of the stone.
Her shawl, or what is left of it.
clues.journal: A rag of her Larkfold shawl was tied at the head of the stone.

escort_cass.goal: Walk Cass down off the moor to {place:hollow}
escort_cass.journal: Cass came down off the moor, past the old ditch where her village had walked. She did not look at it, and she did not hurry.

camp_one.goal: Make a fire for the night at {place:hollow}

give.name: Cass's kindling
lore: A bundle from under her shawl: three sticks to cross and one to stand up.
Dry, for all the moor is wet.

fire_one.goal: Sit the night at the fire with Cass

lines.say: Three sticks crossed and one stood up in the middle. That is a Larkfold fire. I have not sat at one in two winters.
The fire catches and settles. Cass sits with her back to the moor and to the old ditch.
There are twenty-two of them, and I have not said one aloud since the night it burned. If I come to the hall with my mouth cold I shall stop at the third and stand there like a post.
So I'll say one at each fire, going down, to get my tongue round them. You need not answer. You did not know them.
Harry Coombe. The miller. He laughed so that you heard it at the far end of the street, and he gave short weight to nobody but the priest.
He put me in the meal bin when they came, and shut the lid, and sat down on it. That is why I was the one they found last. I have never got the flour out of this shawl.
My boy's second name is Harry. I have never told {raider} why. He thinks it is for an uncle.
She says the name once more, under her breath. The flame leans towards her, though there is no wind in the hollow.
That is one. Sleep, if you can. I'll watch the first half.

fire_one.journal: At the first fire Cass said one of Larkfold's names aloud: Harry Coombe, the miller. She means to say one at every fire on the way down.

walk_two.goal: Walk Cass on down the road to {place:fork}

camp_two.goal: Make a fire for the night at {place:fork}

give.name: Cass's kindling
lore: A bundle from under her shawl: three sticks to cross and one to stand up.
She gathered it on the way down and said nothing about it.

fire_two.goal: Sit the night at the fire with Cass

lines.say: Cass kneels at the waystone and puts her hand into the hollow under it, where the pot was.
He put it here on his way up, in case, with a day or two of fire still in it. He could have carried it on to the camp and lost it with the purse. He left a coal where somebody would find it.
Ada Wren. She kept the geese, and one of them bit the priest, and she said it had better judgment than the whole street.
She worked a wren on every shawl she owned, so that nobody could say they had taken hers by mistake.
Cass looks across the fire for a long moment. She does not ask who walked at the old ditch, or who put them down.
Up at the camp I kept my teeth shut on them, so that nobody there should have the use of them. I had forgotten they would still come when called.
When the boy is old enough I shall say them to him at our own fire, one a night, like this. Somebody ought to say them up there, of all places.
That is two. Twenty yet, and then his. I can do twenty. I think I can do twenty.
The fire burns down to a red eye. A long way down the road there is one light, where the town is.

fire_two.journal: At the waystone fire Cass said the second: Ada Wren, who kept the geese and worked a wren on every shawl. Twenty left to say, and then her father's.

rite.goal: Light the Larkfold coal from the hall's fire and set it in the hearth

journal.?cass=dead: The Larkfold coal was lit again from the Hearthkeeper's fire, and the names were said by a stranger. Cass's name was said last, and her father's under it.
journal.?mark:ch_alone: The Larkfold coal was lit again from the Hearthkeeper's fire, and the names were said by a stranger.
journal.?: The Larkfold coal was lit again from the Hearthkeeper's fire, and Cass Marten said the names of her dead aloud, every one.

?cass=dead: It is lit. Now the names. Say them slowly, so she has time to see each face. You did not know the faces. Say them anyway.
You have put the girl on the end. Cass Marten. And her father under her. Good. She heard that. I felt the fire lean.
?mark:ch_alone: It is lit. Now the names. Say them slowly, so she has time to see each face. You did not know the faces. Say them anyway.
Twenty-two. And the thatcher, last. It is not the same as kin. It is something. She heard something.
?cass=wed: It is lit, and she said them all, every one, and told me a thing about each: the miller's laugh, the Wren girls' goose that bit the priest. She did not cry until her father's name. Then she did.
She is sitting by the door with her shawl on. She has not taken it off since she came in. She is waiting for you to walk her home.
?: It is lit, and she said them all, every one, and told me a thing about each: the miller's laugh, the Wren girls' goose that bit the priest. She did not cry until her father's name. Then she did.
She says she has nowhere to go. I have told her the hall always wants hands. She has not answered. Let her be a while.

replies.say: Say Edwy Marten's name last of all.
replies.journal: Edwy Marten's name was said last of all, at the Hearthkeeper's fire.

returns.say: I cut the thatcher's name in the hearthstone last of all, as you asked, a little apart from the others, the way he walked. The Larkfold coal has not once gone dim. A guest at her hearth is given bread and honey, and you were her guest that night whether you knew it or not.

replies.say: It is done. Let them rest.
Don't go back up the moor, Cass. Stay down here, where it is safe.
replies.journal: The promise to Cass was broken. She was told to stay at the hall and not go back to the camp.

returns.say: You swore to her. Down and back up, she said you swore it. She walked the moor alone in the dark to keep your promise for you, and she has not been well since. I came down myself to see what kind of thing breaks its word to a girl with a dead father.

escort_back.goal: Walk Cass back up to {place:tents}, as promised
escort_back.journal: Cass was walked back up the moor to her own fire, as promised.

lines: We are home. This is home. The boy did not know me for a whole morning, and then he would not let go of my hair.
{raider} says you are welcome at our fire, once, and after that you are a stranger like anybody. That is a great deal, from him.
I said their names. I said my father's. I will say them to the boy when he is old enough to hold the pot. Thank you for walking slow.

?mark:ch_broke: Cass sat by our hearth three nights and would not eat. On the fourth she walked up onto the moor alone, in the dark, with her shawl over her head.
{raider} met her at the old ditch, the drovers say, and carried her the last of the way. He has sent word down the drove road asking who it was that kept her. I did not tell him. Somebody will.
?cass=dead: The Larkfold coal has burned a week in the Hearthkeeper's fire and has not once gone dim. Nothing has walked at the old ditch since. The drovers say it is quieter down there than it has been in two winters.
I cut Cass Marten's name in the hearthstone with the others, and her father's under it. Somebody from the moor camp left a sprig of heather on our step. I do not know who.
?mark:ch_alone: The Larkfold coal has burned a week in the Hearthkeeper's fire and has not once gone dim. Nothing has walked at the old ditch since.
I cut the names in the hearthstone, and the thatcher's last. There is a space left under his. I did not know what to put there, so I have left it.
?: The Larkfold coal has burned a week in the Hearthkeeper's fire and has not once gone dim. Nothing has walked at the old ditch since.

Cass is with us. She carries water and keeps the fire and says the names to it every night before she sleeps. Last night she laughed at something one of the novices said, and then looked surprised at herself.

forgotten.text: The Larkfold hearth-pot was left cold with the hall-keeper, and nobody went looking for Cass.

lost_on_road.text: Cass Marten died on the road between the moor and the hearth-hall, with her father's names unsaid.

text.?mark:ch_bought: Cass Marten was bought out of the raiders' camp and said her village's names at the Hearthkeeper's fire. She keeps that fire now.
text.?: Cass Marten was taken out of the raiders' camp at a blade's point and said her village's names at the Hearthkeeper's fire. She keeps that fire now.

town: There's a red-haired girl at the hearth-hall says names to the fire every night. Larkfold, she says. Never heard of it.
Raiders' camp on the moor's been quiet. Counting their losses, I expect.

returns.say: The hall-keeper let me carry the coal at midwinter, to light the new year from it. I always wanted to, and Father never once let me. I have finished the bird. He did the wings. I did the head. It is not very good. It is yours.

there_and_back.text: Cass Marten said her village's names at the Hearthkeeper's fire and was walked back up to her own fire on the moor, as was promised.
town: Somebody walked a girl from the moor camp into the hearth-hall and out again. A raider's woman, at our fire.
Larkfold? Burned two winters back. Didn't know anybody was left.

promise_broken.text: Cass Marten said her village's names at the Hearthkeeper's fire, and was kept from going home against her word. She walked back up the moor alone.
town: That moor girl walked off from the hearth-hall in the dark. All on her own. Who lets a girl do that?
There's a raider been asking on the drove road for somebody. Wouldn't want to be them.

text.?cass=dead: Cass Marten was found under a stone at the raiders' camp. A stranger said Larkfold's names at the Hearthkeeper's fire, with hers last, and her father's under it.
text.?: Larkfold's names were said at the Hearthkeeper's fire by a stranger. Cass Marten stayed at the raiders' camp and never heard them said.

town: The hearth-hall's cut a new row of names in the stone. Some village nobody remembers.
Quiet at the old ditch now. The drovers go that way again.
